utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today we find ourselves again in a situation where for urgent personal reasons Judge Fluegge is unable to sit, and Judge Moloto and myself have decided that it's in the interest of justice to continue to hear the case. We are still confident that this will not take longer than five days. Therefore, we'll proceed. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. There are no preliminaries as far as I'm aware of. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honour, everyone. As you recall, you asked me to consider the correctness of a citation yesterday made by Mr. Ivetic, and it was -- in fact, I can confirm it was a correct citation to the Popovic judgement -- or excuse me, the Popovic transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's hereby on the record. Mr. Ivetic, as I understood, you would finish within half an hour let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you again that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination and he announced, just for you to know, he will need about half an hour. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday we left off at the incident on the 12th of July when there was an encounter that you described between General Mladic and the Muslim interpreter for Bravo Company that had been acting as your interpreter during the day, and I want to ask you prior to that time, how long had you been operating in a heightened state of stress and how little or how much sleep had you gotten?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the evening of the 9th that I went to the blocking position, until then of course I was working in stressful situations, and I think during those days and nights I had some cat-naps, so a few hours of sleep in total, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now talking about this Muslim UN interpreter, do you know would the same or similar likely have been true for him at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At page 42 of P1154, your Rule 92 ter statement, you describe the Muslim interpreter after the encounter, and I'd like to direct to that if I may. I apologise, one page prior. And at lines 12 through 15 you state the following: "He was incredibly scared, shivering, literally shivering all of his body. And he was actually so scared that I decided to take [sic] him back escorted -- let him be escorted back to the compound because he was not able to be there any more." Do you consider that given the circumstances and the condition that the interpreter was in that the exact words of General Mladic may have been somewhat haphazardly interpreted to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking for expert opinion, more or less, Mr. Ivetic. We will ask the witness to answer the question, but just for you to be aware of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know, but in the way the interpreter spoke to me during the conversation, it didn't seem to me that he was in a different state of mind than he was during the day-time, and during that day he did all the interpreting for me. So I had no -- no reason to doubt that his interpretations were different from what he had done the rest of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And just for the record, you at that point in time did not have any ability or knowledge to speak the Serbo-Croatian language; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's accurate. Only a few words but no sentence or whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can't eat your cake and have it, Mr. Ivetic. Either you ask the witness whether he was able to assess the accuracy of the translation under the circumstance and then to say, Well, but you didn't know the language, is a bit problematic for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I wasn't asking to assess the translation. I was asking did he consider, did the witness consider the circumstances to have had an effect on the translator such that he did not have faith in the translation. That's what I was asking him. I was asking this witness what he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then he said I didn't consider the translation any different or any doubts, and then you said but you don't speak the language. That's actually the gist of what you're doing. But please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to how the translator was translating the rest of the day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, are you aware, sir, that someone that same day had shot some weapon rounds at General Mladic in Srebrenica trying to kill him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the time that you asked the interpreter to approach General Mladic, the interpreter was dressed in civilian clothing and without any UN soldiers accompanying him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was General Mladic surrounded by his bodyguards or standing away from them?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his bodyguards were not close to him at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I appreciate at the time you didn't think or consider it, but looking back at the situation now, do you perhaps concede that it was a risky decision sending the translator dressed in civilian clothes without any UN soldiers to talk directly to General Mladic such that he could be considered as a potential threat to the safety of General Mladic by him or by the bodyguards?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, looking back, I think also the physical condition and the appearance of the translator I would say that looking back I would still think it was very risky situation for the translator to do that. That's why he also hesitated. And the whole situation was a risky one also for myself, of course, but looking back, no, I don't think there was any threat coming from the translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did the translator ever tell you exactly what he had told General Mladic when he approached him, the actual words that were conveyed?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of my colleagues on the other side, I'd like to show you a short video-clip. For the record it will be part of P1147, and I believe the Prosecution should have the first clip. It's from 00:23:30 to 00:23:54. It's a short 20-odd second clip. And, sir, as you watch this clip with me I'd like you to pay particular attention to the translator who is doing the translation and also the subtitles of the translations so that we can see what is being said here and then I'll save my questions for afterwards, and I want to find out if this translator is the Muslim translator that we have been talking about. So if we could please play the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "He says that all -- all of the people [indiscernible]."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, having played the clip, were you able to identify the translator who is providing translation between Lieutenant Koster and General Mladic as being the Muslim translator that we have been talking up until now?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is not the Muslim interpreter that was interpreting for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. And now I'd like to look at P1148, which is the Srebrenica stills book. We're moving on to another topic. Just for the record, I think it was evident that the -- from looking at the subtitles and the transcript of the video that that particular interpreter which is not the one that we're talking about was incorrectly interpreting between Lieutenant Koster and General Mladic. But now I'd like to move on to stills book and we looked at page 105 in the hard copy which is page 117 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I can imagine that you want to put on the record that the Defence has concern about the accuracy rather than that you testified that it was not okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's now clear on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, looking at this page of the stills book, is this a -- there's yourself to the right and the gentleman with the number 2 on his chest. Is this a picture of the person that you have referred as to the translator Miki?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you see the identifications on the bottom of this page identifying both Miki and the individual to the left as being members of the police? Was that your understanding at the time that Miki was a policeman rather than an official translator?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time they told me that he was not an official translator but could speak English and he could ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Are you done? I thought you were going to say something after "he could," or ...

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could speak English. That was -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to review a part of the Popovic trial transcript with you to see if it is accurately reciting something in relation to this encounter. I'd call up 1D897 and ask for page 55 in e-court, which correlates to page 2366 of the Popovic transcript and if we can begin with line 17. Oops, actually -- yes, 17. And if you could follow along, sir: "Q. [Interpretation] Major, I think that yesterday we froze the footage at this precise frame. You recognise Mane, you recognise the interpreter Miki, and you are also in the shot. Can you see the subtitles on this frame, where they say, 'And to check and see whether anybody wants to go. It's their job.' "Since we cannot determine from the subtitles who is saying what, whose words they are, can we please confirm the following: These words are directed by Captain Mane to the interpreter Miki, is that right, so that he could interpret them to you. Is that the right interpretation of what we are seeing here? "A. From what I saw in the video clipping, that is the correct course of events. "Q. Thank you very much. "Judge Agius: If you want to -- a couple of seconds, I think it will be clear. Because you here a voice calling Miki and then it continues from there. Then they play the video-tape. "Judge Agius: I think it's clear enough. "Mr. Lazarevic: Yes, I think so. "Judge Agius: Thank you. "Mr. Lazarevic: "Q. Mane says to Miki to tell you that you should see whether there was anyone else who wished to leave. Does this refer to the refugees who were there? "A. If I read the subtitles, it would refer to the refugees, but if I remember correctly, this phrase was not translated to me by Miki. "Q. No. Thank you. So it's more or less what's being said. But actually, what I'm interested in is that you did have problems with interpretation, especially when this man named Miki was interpreting? "A. I don't have a way to control if Miki was telling exactly what Mane was -- wanted to tell me because I don't speak Serbo-Croatian. "Q. Right. So you're saying you can't be 100 per cent sure that what Miki said was perfectly exactly interpreted by -- sorry, that what Mane said was perfectly interpreted by Miki?" And the answer's on the next page: "A. No, I don't have to have a way or did not have a way there to control it, but I'm sure that if things would go in a different way than Mane wanted, he would have objected and would have told Miki that he wanted it otherwise. But I don't have a way to control if it was the exact or perfect translation that Mane wanted." Now, sir, does this selection accurately and truthful comport with your memory of the testimony that you gave in the Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's accurate and truthful, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if I understand correctly, these words from Mane or anything resembling these words were never passed along to you by Miki or were incorrectly translated to you Miki. Is that -- is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that sentence, that specific sentence, and especially the part where Mane says "It's their job." I do not remember that that sentence was translated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And now I'd again with the assistance of the Office of the Prosecutor, I'd like to play a clip from the video-tape. This will be the third clip that I had announced. That is from V-009267-1-A, from 00:05:47 to 00:06:40. And if we can play the clip the question I would ask you to keep in mind, sir, is: Is this the segment that you recall was the subject of this discussion in the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so, sir, now having viewed the video is this the video segment that was the subject of this exchange in the Popovic trial that we've just went through?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I can see it it's that part, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as you went with the interpreter towards the water truck, Mane did not come with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember Mane as seen there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that now looking back at the situation and the actual words that were spoken now having been translated by professional translators, that there was a lot of room for misinterpretation and error for English-speaking persons relying upon this translator at the site?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when you speak about this translator you refer to Miki?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Miki.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There -- there could be some room for other interpretation by Miki, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to be clear, was Miki the person who interpreted the words of Mane at the white house in relation to the passports?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to play one more clip with the help of the Office of the Prosecutor, and it would be the second clip that I had announced which is, for the record, part of P1147. It is the video V-000-9266-1-A, and it begins at 00:23:54 and goes until 00:24:29. And I want to urge to pay attention to the words being spoken by General Mladic to the refugees, and if we could play the clip then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, are these words uttered by General Mladic to the civilian refugees and their responses to him something that you were made aware of or witnessed in Potocari; that is to say, did the translators provide you with such information about how Mladic was addressing the crowd of refugees?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard about this, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for answering my questions. Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. McCloskey, any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. van Duijn, since the Bench has no further questions for you either, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much and often I say coming from far away, but that perhaps not applies to you, but I thank you nevertheless for coming to this courtroom and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And even if it's a short distance I wish you safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe we have the continuing cross-examination of Mr. Ruez, who should be behind me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ruez. Mr. Ruez, perhaps needless to say, but of course you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The cross-examination will now be continued. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's resume, and I'll call up your exhibit in e-court, P1132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic and the parties, the witness was provided with a list of names and numbers, and I do understand -- I don't know whether you want to use it, but the witness doesn't have it at his disposition at this moment, so if there's any need to use, I would say, the codes, then he should be provided with it. Again, if there's no need --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware for now that I'm going to use the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that a copy has been provided to the witness, so if there is any need for him to refer to any of those persons, then he now has the tool he needs for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are still waiting for P1132. And we'll need page 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's page 58 in your book if you want to use hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we can see here is an aerial image of Nova Kasaba. The markings indicate the areas that can be seen in the next image. The date here is the 13th of July, 1995. And we need the next page, page 78 in e-court. Here an indication is made of soil disturbance. We can see that it's the 27th of July, 1995, and it's another aerial image. There are no survivors from these sites, no survivors of possible executions; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is right. There are no survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that one cannot rule out the possibility that these people or some of them were killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want my personal opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want your opinion. I want the information that your investigation team arrived at. Was this a possibility that could be ruled out as a result of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I will in the shortest possible explain you what the investigation tells us about this site. One witness who was a trying to escape from this large hill and cross the asphalt road was hiding himself at the bottom of an electric pylon and had a sight in between two houses. From there he could see two armoured vehicles on the road. He saw the first group of 30 people marched on a meadow where they were lined up. Men equipped with automatic rifles stood on the APCs and shot this group. This witness stayed. A short time later a second group arrived, was lined up among the bodies of the first group, and they were shot. In between, the soldiers were shouting, shooting in the air. And then a third group arrived. The witness left the area. It took us four years to find the location this witness was talking about, because on this stretch of road of approximately 3 kilometres, there were many possible locations. So we went from north to south, and fortunately the last possibility was the south. The description of the location is visible on the photograph. At the top left of the red square you have two houses. Unfortunately, the pylon is not visible. It would be approximately located where the A of "Areas" is. At some point late 2000, I think, during the summer 2000, this meadow, the last one we searched, was scooped with metal detectors and a large number of bullets were found embedded into the ground. There is a report from my colleagues who did this search in my absence because it was at the last stage of the mission and I did leave the area. Meanwhile, they were conducting this operation. So in my view, due to the proximity of the location of these graves, these graves might be the graves where the bodies of these people have been dumped into. There is another grave a little bit more north of this location that we didn't show for the sake of this trial, which is hidden from the road by a tree -- a very thick tree-line where the exhumation report will say how many bodies have been found. I do not remember precisely. So my assumption is that these graves contain the bodies of the -- at least of this execution, not -- maybe not only this one but at least of this one. Then regarding the possibility that these people inside the graves were battle casualties, from the photographs I took on the -- the probe -- of the probe that we did on the grave that is located just at the bottom left of this red box, as I have shown, the most obvious body was in civilian clothes and had his hands tied with wire. I have hard -- I have difficulties thinking that a man with the hands bounded with a wire in his back has been killed in combat, but it's my opinion. There is a full exhumation report on this that Professor Wright will detail for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you could rule out the possibility that -- that among those buried this these graves were also people killed in combat. Can you rule that possibility out or not? That's all. And then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question has been answered by the witness. He says there may have been others than from those execution, and I do understand he has not excluded that those others may have been killed in combat. Is that right, Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is right, and Professor Wright will give more very interesting details regarding these graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I will move on. [Interpretation] We now need page 92 in e-court. I apologise. We need page 84. It's Konjevic Polje. I apologise. I can't find it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you do remember that in connection with Konjevic Polje there were quite a few single graves or graves containing two or three bodies; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found one containing one single body, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you add anything about graves with two or three bodies, because that was part of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- we were looking for small graves in this area in order to implement witness testimonies claiming that they saw people surrendering and that those carrying weapons had to dig their grave and were shot inside. Purely a witness assessment. So we probed several locations in this area to find small graves, and we could find one with one individual inside, and the report done of it by Professor Wright, and he was the one, concludes that the hole in which this body was found was hand-dug. It's the only possible implementation that we could have of these bits of stories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, so the short answer is that you did not find graves with two or three bodies in it. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, one, but not two or three, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That would have been the short answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that even this one was worth mentioning, this individual one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had mentioned it already in your first answer. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now deal with the Kravica warehouse. On the issue of Kravica, as well as other areas, is it correct that many of the sites that you investigated were in fact within a war zone?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The damage to the buildings that were the warehouse at Kravica could actually be ascribed to war activities, could it not?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this type of damages in a war zone could indeed be caused by war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of your investigation, you also came by information that in Kravica on the Orthodox Christmas day in 1993, Serbian civilians were attacked and massacred; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have information that indeed during the Orthodox Christmas day of 1993, there was an attack on Kravica where a certain number of people have been killed, but I did not investigate this matter and would not say if these people were military or civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you learn in the course of your investigation that in July of 1995 there were quite a few revenge motivated murders?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you come by information -- or, rather, in this area of Konjevic Polje was this information related to a lot of isolated murders or groups of people killed? I'm sorry, not Konjevic Polje. I meant Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the revenge aspect is concerned, I would more spot these things in Bratunac town. Kravica warehouse is not something committed by lonely individuals, isolated individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This applies to the Kravica warehouse. I meant the area around Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To summarise a large number of witness testimonies, those driving along the road, individual bodies were spotted on -- on the way. So these lonely murders happened all along the stretch of road. Kravica warehouse involves a very large number of victims, and I think the situation in Kravica has been already went through in details during -- I mean during the presentation, but even much more during previous trials. I'm sure you know all these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the warehouse in Kravica, is it correct that as prisoners arrived there the atmosphere was relaxed, but that at one point the armed Serb guards, members of the police, had two automatic rifles seized from them by the Muslims who were in the warehouse and that one of the two guards was killed, the other wounded?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the relaxed ambience, I would not use these words, but indeed I heard the story about the fact that one of the soldiers had his hands burned when he -- he grabbed a rifle, but I need to say that as you know, the execution there, which is not in Kravica itself. In Kravica itself there is another warehouse destroyed by war damage. We never used it for the sake of any trial because it's not connected with any execution. This warehouse is very -- at the exit of Kravica. So it's not the warehouse in Kravica village. It's very away of the village. Since the events in Kravica happened in two waves, we can split them in two parts, first the execution west, then later the execution east. Though the fact that a soldier was killed nearby and one had his hand burnt on the spot, I see that what you mean that it would be a reaction of angry soldiers who want to revenge their comrade. I don't know. I cannot tell you what was the exact reason, but it's not exactly like this, but I personally feel the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, the second part of your answer you more or less confirmed that there was a story about a soldier killed. Did the investigation reveal any further information about when and where a soldier was wounded and a soldier was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the time I did the investigation, the only thing we could observe is that there is a little memorial nearby, very close to Sandici, to the name of apparently this soldier who was killed the 13, as far as I know, because I learned that after I left the Tribunal, the event of the killed soldier, as well as the story regarding the burnt hands. This was not during the six years I was busy with the investigation. I found out later by my conversations with my former colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the question suggested that it was related to the Kravica warehouse. Did the investigation confirm that the person, the soldier killed, and the soldier burned or wounded, that that happened at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The burned hand at the warehouse, but the shooting of -- the death of this soldier not at the warehouse, nearby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you consider nearby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the meadow, so less than 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will be the subject of -- of the testimony and probably some fundamental agreement on these interesting issues between the Defence and Prosecution, just so you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but since Mr. Lukic raises the matter, I would like to understand the answers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] It's time for the break, Your Honour, I think. It's half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I missed what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's time for break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Time for a break. Yes. Yes. We'll take a break, and we -- but first we invite the witness to follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, there was a reference to soldiers in Kravica, but is your information that there were representatives of the police, not of the Army of Republika Srpska, were present there?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, the presence was the presence of the Special Police Brigade and of the command of Colonel Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move on to the area of Zvornik. I'd like to ask you something about Orahovac, the school in Grbavci, in relates to Lazete 1 and 2 as potential execution sites. The school in Grbavci was used by the army for keeping their troops there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is right. From time to time army personnel was using this school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The waste that was in front of the school and that you analysed is not necessarily linked to what happened in July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. Since as you will have the forensic explanation by one team member who specialised in the matter, the blindfolds that were found at the school match the blindfolds that were found in the grave. They match also those found at the dump site, and at a later stage, they match those found in the secondary graves linked with this site.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it correct that none of the detainees at school had heard bursts of gunfire in the vicinity of the school -- or, rather, at the locations of Lazete 1 and Lazete 2?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, it is correct that people who had allegedly survived an execution could not recognise locations at Lazete?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the reasons I already exposed in my direct examination, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At these locations, Lazete 1 and Lazete 2, a total of 493 bodies were found. Do you recall that piece of information right now? If not, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept your number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you something about the school in Petkovci. We need P1132 in e-court, page 167. You do know what we're talking about, the blackboard in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you investigate at all whether these are -- this is damage that was caused by bullets?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't take the board with us. The only thing I could say is that the -- the holes in the board could very well match bullet holes, and this could - I say could - implement the witness testimony, regarding the fact that they were shot from time to time, fired from the outside to the inside if people why standing up to get more air.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm pausing just in order to allow the interpretation to finish. Also, you did not find any bullets there, and you didn't even look for them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not -- it's half correct. It's not correct at all, in fact. We did look for bullets, but as I said, this place had been fully refurbished by a NGO before our arrival, so finding bullets in this place was not possible. It had been refurbished, renovated, at the exception of this board.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was not clear enough. In the blackboard itself, you did not find any bullets, and you didn't look for them either?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. We did not take off this board from the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, is it correct that this area was the scene of heavy fighting in 1992? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask something about the school in Rocevic. We need photograph 187, just to be reminded of what it is about. We need 187 in e-court, that is. Now that we're on the subject of this school as a detention location, you personally did not investigate anything that had to do with this school in Rocevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was not done by your investigation team either while you still worked for the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I took this photograph just in anticipation we would at a later stage connect this school with the events we are investigating, but the -- the testimonies connected to military presence in this school by those who were guarding the prisoners at that school happened after my departure in 2001. So I was personally not in a position to investigate anything there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the time being, we won't be needing this any more, so let us remove this from our screens so as not to distract the witness. In your investigations did you come to the following information, that before Krivaja 95 in the area of Srebrenica there were constant offensive operations takes place against the Serb villages? These operations were carried out by the 28th Division of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that you did not investigate this, but as background information did you know how many Serbs were killed in these operations carried out by the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The usual number that comes up by those talking about these events between 1992 and 1995 involving the Serb victims is usually 2.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you establish -- or, actually, did you deal with this at all, how many people were within Srebrenica before Krivaja 95 started? Do you have precise information about that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two questions, one regarding if I dealt with this aspect. The answer, as you know, is no. Investigation for me starts in 11 July 1995, the fall of Srebrenica. As far as the second one is concerned, the usual number from various sources, UN, NGO, Medecins sans Frontieres, the UN battalion, and so on, was about 45.000 within the enclave, if I remember well. But -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't deal with that, although we have a Muslim document from that period of time, and it says 36.000.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I understand this as that you agree with the existence of a Muslim document which says 36.000, or is it -- or do you say that's the right number and all the others, the 45.000, are wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My real answer on this is that -- and I might have to repeat it, is that in my eyes, what I consider my duty in this investigation is to determine the number of people who have been assassinated, the victims who have been first captured who were prisoners and executed, and then calculations regarding the number of people within the enclave. I accept the number of 36 without any difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But earlier you said on average the estimates are at 45.000. Now, if you say, "I accept 36," is that because you consider this a better estimate, or -- or one of the estimates existing on the lower side of the range? How do we have to understand that you accept something here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might be between 36.000 and 45.000. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Knowing how many people were inside the enclave before the fall of the enclave has not been my primary concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd say you have no reasons to believe that it's certainly wrong. It may be right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as the 45.000, that may be right at well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your investigation, did you find out how many people died in Srebrenica during the course of the war or were killed during the war, in Srebrenica itself, that is?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer will be exactly the same as previously. For sure people died between 1992 and 1995. Others died in combat. Some died from diseases, whatever, yes. I didn't investigate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you did not know the exact number of people who had assembled in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precise number, no. I would let you rely on testimonies provided by members of the UN battalion who have certainly an estimate of this. I remember 5.000 sheltered inside the main base, and some -- I don't remember how many outside. I would leave them to provide you with a more precise estimate. We had one, but I don't remember it by heart. It's an estimate anyhow. Nobody was there to count precisely the crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So all of these figures that we referred to until now are tentative. They were never determined precisely, or at least not by your team. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is it really a serious question whether it was ever established precisely by counting how many people were in the compound and outside the compound? We have seen the pictures. How is this a serious question or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was not related, at least I hope, only to Potocari but to the number of inhabitants in Srebrenica, number of killed, number of died people in Srebrenica during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All are estimates. All are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- ask about that. What you said is "so all of these figures," that includes the assessment of the number of people in the compound and outside of that. So if you want to know whether the population was counted, then you can ask for it. At the same time, after we've heard the evidence about when the witness says 36.000 could be right, 45.000 could be right, that already indicates that there was no such counting done. So if you want to have further detailed information, put focused questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I think in relation to this you cannot give us precise information about the number of killed persons in Srebrenica or the number of members of the 28th Division who lost their lives during the war and also about the number of inhabitants in Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely right, because this was not connected to the events I was in charge of investigating.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Did you establish how many members of the 28th Division were killed in fighting with the Serb forces, or in the shelling of the column that was attempting to break through to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you something about the initial contacts that you had with the Muslim side when you started working. You contacted the authorities in Sarajevo when you arrived in BH in July 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not right. I arrived -- I arrived through Split on the coast, and I flew in directly to Tuzla by helicopter. I didn't go through Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was not right. I meant the authorities in Sarajevo, the Sarajevo authorities. I'm saying you did not establish contact with the authorities of Republika Srpska or the military; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This contact was made precisely with a view to investigating the Srebrenica case, this contact with the authorities of the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initial goal of the mission was to assess the credibility of the -- what I will call the press rumour claiming that 8.000 people had disappeared following the fall of the enclave and that there was at least one account of the mass execution that led the opinion of those who were covering the events to believe that, in fact, the disappeared people had been killed. This was the initial situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Through the authorities on the Muslim side, you got in touch with witnesses as well; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You contacted members of the 2nd Corps, right, the one stationed in Tuzla, the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at stage. Not in July and August 1995. Later. The 2nd Corps was much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D849. Could we please take a look at that. Could we have it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see the B/C/S version in front of us. We were be looking at this document of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 2nd Corps, and it contains instructions as to how the methodology should be used, the methodology for questioning witnesses, that is. Did you have anything to do with that, how information was to be collected, because this document is dated the 10th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. During the summer 1995, we interviewed -- I say "we" because we were two persons interviewing. It was me and Mrs. Sue Castro. We were only two personnel during that summer, and we were later joined by Mr. Papean, Jos Papean. So I interviewed, I remember, one 28 Division member who had nothing to say because he escaped. He went through all the military events between 13 and 16 July, but the military events were not the topic of our investigation. We were trying to find out what happened to the, in brackets, disappeared persons. So this military episode was of no concern. It might be that few more persons were -- from the 28 Division have been interviewed maybe by Jos Papean or Sue Castro, but we had no interest for this. Our main concern was to find witnesses of three things: The events in Potocari, that was the first group of persons we tried to identify; second group, what happened during the evacuation, the 12 and the 13, all along the stretch of road --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be a need to consult with Mr. Mladic who wants to remain seated and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking. Whispering. It's still audible, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, this is the last time that we accept Mr. Mladic speaking at such a volume. Otherwise, he'll have to wait until the break, and we'll not allow you to consult any further. So it's up to Mr. Mladic either to lower his volume. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't finish my sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was -- sorry for interrupting you. My question was whether you have anything to do with this order of 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discover this document. I'm going to read it. Give me the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I must try to follow what you are trying to do here. This is a letter of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know what the date of the letter is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 10th of August, 1995. Just a second. Are you saying that this letter is a letter according to which this witness is supposed to have collected information when he was investigating?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to keep matters simple. Did you ever receive any instructions as what format you should use when you would interview witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In no way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was the opposite one. Did this gentleman provide guidelines as to Army of B and H --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's totally unclear. Did you ever suggest how members of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina would have to conduct their interviews and what format they should use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never ever. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. That's an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also to mine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Yes, but if you put it clearly, you get an answer clear and quickly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to ask you about the intercepts, the ones taken by the Muslim side. Already in 1995 you heard that the BH authorities had intercepts in their possession; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You asked for that documentation for the first time on the 13th of November, 1996. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We have the chain of custody of the documentation. You were not told at the time how many such intercepts there were; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were not told what the intercepts contained either; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you received some of these intercepts for the first time only in March 1998?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true, because we did not receive them. In fact, we found them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, is there any dispute about these matters? Apparently it is recorded. It has been -- has been disclosed to the Defence. Have you ever sat together to see whether there's any dispute about these matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have not, and I don't think there fundamentally is, though the date's so long ago I think there's some memory issues about actual dates, but the process is -- has been open and agreed upon for years fundamentally. The intercepts and their content may have been in issue, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Lukic, why not focus on what is in dispute rather than matters which apparently are not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since this gentleman had first-hand knowledge about the hand-over of these intercepts, we think it's appropriate to ask him about this, because when he is gone, when he leaves the stand, we will not be able to establish the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if it's not in dispute, if you want to present evidence by first-hand witnesses on matters which are not in dispute, then you reserve your agenda until 2030. I mean, if there's agreement, why -- unless there's any additional question, were they in a blue box or were they in a green box or whatever there is, but if there are matters, when did you for the first time ask? When did you receive the first one? Was it a complete set? These seem to be matters which are, I take it, well recorded, and apparently you rely on that information when putting these questions to the witness. So, therefore, I don't see the point. P. Lease proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't find the trace that it agreed in another case and I don't remember that it's agreed in this case either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then check with the Prosecution whether you can agree on it. That is what your task is, to see where there is dispute, where there's no dispute, so that you can present the evidence on matters where the Chamber will have to decide and not on matters where the parties do not disagree. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what form did you receive these intercepts, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness said they found the intercepts. They didn't receive them. "In what form did you find these intercepts?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the form of little leaflets, handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian authorities ever send an explanation as to why so much time elapsed before you gained possession of these leaflets?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't ask them to provide the information, because as I said, we found them. So we didn't need to ask them why we didn't get them before, because there was no need to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move to a different topic now. I'll put some additional questions to you about the methodology that you used. Primarily, let's establish this: You never worked for the Defence on this case, you worked for the Prosecution, right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's make the things very clear. I was an employee of the OTP, paid by the United Nations. In France, when we conduct an investigation, we say, we do it, I speak French, "a charge et a decharge," meaning that we look for the information that might help accusing someone, but we systematically look into what would also provide elements that he's innocent. It's a question of mentality. Therefore, as I said, some of the witness testimonies we could implement, others we could not. And then we use -- I mean, the Prosecution uses or not the information that we collect. But in fact, yes, I worked for the Prosecution. But what I explain is that it's not because you work for the Prosecution that you act in a biased way, because I see what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did I ask you this? Above all, I wanted us to confirm again that you only investigated the crimes committed against the Muslims and not the crimes against the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my task. My mandate, if I can say so, as I told you, was to investigate the rumour about the disappearance of 8.000 individuals happening to be from the Muslim side. Had I received another task, I would have tried to fulfil that task, but my task was that one and only that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you, well, as you tell us, investigated both those issues that could incriminate or exculpate anyone. Did you also investigate how many people who were moving in the column were killed by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those killed in combat are not part of a crime. We know that there have been numbers killed. Their bodies were still in the forest on the hills between Potocari and Konjevic Polje during the summer 1996. Meanwhile, me and my team were opening the mass graves connected with the detention sites. A group of Norwegians led by Ms. Elisabeth Rehn were collecting bodies on the hills. These bodies have never been counted for the sake of the Prosecution. These are combat casualties. We do not count combat casualties. I repeat: The only element of this investigation is to investigate crimes. The death in these hills is not connected with any crime, as far as I know. I mean, at least not the last execution we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: Did you hear from the witnesses that you interviewed that members of the 28th Division, some of them killed the Muslims who were moving in the column?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you decided whose story you would double-check and which witness?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also decided which issues would be given priority; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In full discussion with all my team members because it's a collective work, but my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that only the evidence that the Prosecution believed was supportive of their case was led in the courtroom in the previous cases?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean for the trials, yes, but during the investigation, no. If you wish, I can give you an example, short example, that will inform you about the way we were doing the things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will get to that. In the trial Popovic et al., my colleague John Ostojic asked you if you were familiar with the concept called confirmatory bias. Did you in your work know how to avoid any possible hint at you being effected by this confirmatory bias?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I have no recollection of this concept, and I'm really not familiar with it, but what I can tell you also is that, you know, I have absolutely no training in terms of presenting this investigation in a courtroom. I can also tell you that I didn't read one line before coming here of all the previous statements for the simple reason is what I have to say I know -- I know it because I did it. I don't need to revisit the past. I will always give you the honest answer because there is only one in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. We'll proceed. [Interpretation] You said that it should not be the case that one investigator would interview more than one survivor from a site so as not to be contaminated by earlier knowledge. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall very well. I was referring to the situation in July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. There seems to be an audio problem with Mr. Mladic. No loud speaking, Mr. ... It seems to have been fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will have to repeat my question. Is it correct that one investigator should not be interviewing several survivors from a given site, that's to say more than one eyewitness of the same event so as not to be contaminated by previous knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the ideal situation. An example of it, July 1995. July 1995, we were two investigators, I mean two persons taking statements. Let's take the situation of the dam. We have two survivors. I interviewed one. Sue Castro interviewed the second one. It seems purely logical. You do not -- if you can avoid it, you share the things so in order for the future, for the sake of the future, not to be accused being indeed contaminated by the knowledge you have gained from the first one. But this is when you can. Sometimes you can't. If you are alone, you deal with what you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But can we agree that you interviewed three of the four survivors of Orahovica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is unfortunately, right. I did according to the available resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We understand and accept that. You agreed and said that you interviewed these witnesses once again if that was necessary; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, for this type of very high quality witnesses, let's say so, we did spend a day, let's say eight hours, which is honestly nothing, and it was one interview. On some instances I -- there was another interview, for example the survivor of the Kravica warehouse, because the first check I did not find the guard room he was talking about. So this one had to be re-interviewed, because I didn't -- I couldn't be sure that the warehouse was the good warehouse because the inside had been destroyed and we couldn't know that at that time. But I don't think the others were re-interviewed. Maybe. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] I'd now like us to focus on the Vuk Karadzic school. Information about the number of detainees within that school was something you received from Miroslav Deronjic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection having been ever provided with a number within this school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Miroslav Deronjic told you that only one classroom was being used for putting people there within that school?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, Miroslav Deronjic had a natural way of minimising everything, especially his involvement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, the question is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not whether you believe what he said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the question was whether Miroslav Deronjic told you that only one classroom was used for putting people there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember that now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you believe him? Do you believe Miroslav Deronjic was telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My belief, but it's a personal belief that I cannot implement with evidence, is that since a column of buses and trucks was lined in front of the school, my assumption is that the school was full, but I never talked with anyone who was inside, so I cannot say that. But since also this school had already been used in 1992, especially the gym, I don't see why it would not have been used in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you yourself never heard of any evidence that would contradict Miroslav Deronjic's statement?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution has more evidence on this, but this happened after my departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, when you're talking about the buses, the column of buses and trucks lined in front of the school, that is at the occasion where Mr. Deronjic told you that only one classroom was used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The night between the 12th and the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do I understand your testimony to say that I could not draw any definite conclusions on the matter, but if you have several buses and lining -- buses and trucks for the people to be taken from the school or to be delivered to the school or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. On one of the exhibits of the photograph of Bratunac, I showed lines of buses in front of various places, one being in front of -- lined in front of the Vuk Karadzic school. So since the people stayed all night onboard all of these buses and trucks, describing some events also, my assumption is that they stayed in these vehicles because the school was packed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it time for our next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we are about at the point where we take the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because I'm moving to another subject, if it's a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please tell us how much more time you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will probably have to use all my time I asked for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please be so kind to focus on matters which are in dispute and try to be as focused as you can. And if you could remind me on how much time you said you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Five hours. I asked for seven and then I cut it down to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reduced it to five hours. Yes. I'll consult with Madam Registrar on the time already used. Could the witness follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we will resume at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness could be escorted into the courtroom, I have to apologise for the second time this morning a late start which was due to very urgent Tribunal matters which kept me busy for more minutes than I expected. Meanwhile, I also use the time. Mr. Lukic, the whole issue about that letter, one simple question would have done: Did you ever suggest how the BiH authorities would have to use formats for their investigations? If the witness would have said no, then we could have moved on, unless you would have wanted to explore the matter further, but from what I understood, showing the letter, you accepted a no. That letter, there was no suggestion whatsoever that the witness would have been involved in it, unless you have reasons to assume that. If that is the case, you could have asked further questions, but the one simple question would have done it. Mr. Mladic is supposed not to speak aloud as he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what I mean with focused, Mr. Lukic. You may proceed. Mr. Ruez is ready, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Headphones on. Glasses on. [Interpretation] Now I'd like to ask you something about these aerial images from another source. In an exhibit that you compiled, between 200 -- actually, among 271 photographs there are about 36 aerial images, and they were all received from a single agency; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are received from a single agency, yes. For the rest, the numbers you give, I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A matter which apparently is not in dispute that they were received from a single agency?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A single government source would be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So therefore, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have follow-up questions, so I have to establish this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see whether it was really necessary to, but even if you have follow-up questions, if you agree on it, then you don't have to introduce the matter with the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to inquire with Mr. McCloskey, do we have to go to a private session when we discuss this source?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not -- not the aerial images from the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at page 236 from P1132. Page 236 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see it on your screen now, the photograph; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the only photograph from this source that I established had a reference to the source. Do you know why on other photographs, since we have established that they all come from the same source, there is no marking of source as far as these other photographs are concerned?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in these aerial images, these photographs, something was added? You've explained that to us already, who added the orange, who added the yellow. Is it correct that something was removed from them as well, for example, some dates were removed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. We have great trouble hearing Mr. Lukic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this one there is a date, and the yellow markings are the markings I have added to the original picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether anything was removed, isn't it? Do you know whether someone else or you yourself removed anything from the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall. I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D857 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll try to refresh your memory. This is your testimony in the Popovic case on the 14th of September, 2006. We'll need page 71 in e-court. This is what you say, the question is in line 13, [In English] and I quote: "Q. My concern is that some of the photos, for example, didn't have the date, and they had a box that still remained. And my question to you is: Do you know who removed the date, if at all? "A. On some of the pictures ... I used, not as such, but in order to talk about the different events that -- in an area shown by this imagery but that was not initially designed to present that situation, I am the one who erased the dates so that we keep only, let's say, what can be seen on the picture but not the reason why it was given to us."

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. This is the case, for example, for one photograph of Bratunac, I think, where the date was not of importance but what was important is to show the location of some buildings. So, yes, I confirm that on some of them I might have erased the date because the date was not relevant, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why do you think that the date is not relevant?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the goal of the exhibit is to show buildings which are constant features on the ground, that do not move except if destroyed, the date of it is not relevant. As simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who decided to have the date removed? Was that your decision?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you something about taking witness statements. You never made audio or video recordings of witness statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rule is that we audio and/or video record the statements of persons who have the status of suspects. There is no audio and video recording necessary for witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question was not whether it was necessary but whether they were made for a fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: None of the witnesses that you interviewed speak English; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not give a B/C/S version of their statements to any one of the witnesses that you interviewed; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. There was no translation made of the English version of their testimony, but they were -- all of them had a read-back in B/C/S prior signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They signed the English version, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is only one version, the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you something about the methodology that you personally applied. You never compiled a report related to your investigations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made internal reports, but none to be put in the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work you relied upon experts from other fields, because you personally do not have knowledge from the fields of archaeology, anthropology, pathology, ballistics; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a team you compared during the course of your work traces on ammunition that had been found in graves and the weapons that you collected from the brigades that you suspected had taken part in the killings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your team, at least while you were still involved, was not in a position to confirm the suspicions that you had; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wrong. You have to split the matter in two. You are wrong on one thing, which is the lack of comparison. The comparisons were positive between shell casings found on the surface of the execution field when compared with the casings found inside the primary mass grave, and later shell casings found in secondary mass graves enabled us to connect the secondary sites with the primary ones. Where you are right is when you say that the operation of seizure of weapons from suspect brigades were unsuccessful, indeed, but there are possible reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that process did you check the weapons of the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just check something with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you say now here on page 45, lines 21 to 25, you say: "The comparisons were positive," sorry, "between shell casings found on the surface of the execution field when compared with the casings found inside the primary mass grave, and later shell casings found in secondary mass graves enabled us to connect the secondary sites." Were there any shells found in secondary mass graves?
