utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Everything should be plural, killing sites with an S, execution sites with an S, et cetera. Dean Manning is the team member who will expose the entire summary of all these forensic aspects. It is not only the shell casings which enabled these comparisons, but also soil, pollen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I stop you just there. Can you listen to my question. Is it your story, your evidence, shell casings were found on secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what I said, and I repeat it, yes. Shell casings were found on the execution sites on the surface. These shell casings were later compared with those found among the bodies found in the primary mass graves, and then when the secondary mass graves were found, the shell casings found inside the secondary mass graves were compared and enabled to connect secondary with primary, because these shell casings, due to the way the executions were done were spread all over, so mixed with -- some were even found in the mouth of some of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you have changed your evidence slightly. You say now that these shell casings were later compared with those found among the bodies found in the primary graves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, my question is going to be -- is going to change based on that. The shell casings you found in the secondary graves, were they found in the bodies or just in the graves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mixed with the soil and the body parts, mixed with all what was found inside these secondary sites. When heavy machines, heavy equipment, collect the bodies, they take everything. They take the bodies, they take the soil, they take everything what is among it. As I showed the little film about the secondary sites Cancari 12, at one point a person is using a metal detector and we can hear beep, beep. Beep, beep means shell casing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Now I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There may be some misunderstanding about his meaning of casing. It's an informal reference. So I'm not sure exactly if it's clear what he means by casing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could explain, but let me see whether I could summarise what I think it might be. A shell casing is the metal containing -- the metal part containing the propelling explosive which causes the bullet to leave the weapon and is usually thrown out from the weapon and therefore falls on the floor close to the weapon. That is my understanding of what a shell casing is and what a bullet is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we will agree. Even Mr. Lukic agrees on what a bullet is and what a shell casing is. Okay, let's -- well, a matter not further in dispute. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let us go to Potocari mentally, although you hadn't been there. A medical convoy of UNPROFOR arrived in Potocari and they transported the wounded. Is that correct? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The information that you have, does it indicate that these persons are alive to this day?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, did you become aware of the fact that some wounded persons were transferred from Bratunac, i.e., members of the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I accept that. Now I'm going to ask you something about civilians or persons who were in Potocari before and after arriving in the territory that was under BH Army control. So one group went towards Potocari from Srebrenica, and another group that included members of the 28th Division mostly moved in the direction of Tuzla. My question -- actually, you've already answered it, my first question, that you did not know how many people had been in Potocari. However, now I'd like to ask you in addition to that whether you knew how many men there were among these people in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A precise count again is not possible. I remember there was an estimate. I cannot recall. We can see a certain number of them on some of the photographs and footages in Potocari, but I don't remember what the assessment was. I think we had an assessment from the persons of the UN battalion, but I don't recall precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We accept everything, but we're just asking you the following: Do you have this information? The next thing I'd like to ask you is whether you have information as to how many men were singled out in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the separation line no one was counting this -- this number. What we know is that those that we have on footage, all of them are on the missing list, identified by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many of the persons in the film were identified by name? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There will be a specific thing by the Prosecution on this, but the footage with V-550 video shows approximately 20 people, so I know for sure that these 20 are identified. I don't know since when if there are more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you believe that the only valid process in terms of determining the number of victims is to carry out all exhumations and to count the bodies. My question is the following: Is it correct that many secondary graves, as you call them, is in the immediate vicinity of the area where the column passed?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could put it like this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work did you establish exactly how many people had certainly been executed?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the precise data at this stage since it -- the number evolutes according to the ongoing exhumations, but as far as those conducted by the ICTY are concerned, the information I have is that we are now at 6.000-plus-something identified bodies for which we connect the graves with execution sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since we have heard that you were not an expert in the field of pathology, for instance, who did you receive this information from that the possibility is ruled out that these 6.000 persons could not have lost their lives in any other way but through a mass execution?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the process we describe. Yeah, I repeat, because of the process we describe. First we -- based on the witness statements we find the detention sites, the connected execution site, and then through the forensics that would be later developed the connection with these primary mass graves and then the secondary mass graves. So for these ones we have our track, and this track is not the burial of battle casualties. And again I will leave it to the chief exhumator, or our two chief exhumators in order to explain the reasons why these bodies are not battle casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, then, we'll put that question to them. Ultimately the civilian from Potocari had to cross from the Serb to the Muslim side on foot. Did your investigation show that the area these civilians crossed was, in fact, no man's land, which nobody could traverse, either the Serb or the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- what is the question about? We are trying to understand the relevance, but sometimes a bit lost. What are you seeking to establish at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was sometimes presented that it was some kind of harassment of civilian population, that there was no need to drive somebody across that piece of land by any of sides, nor Serb side nor Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is then the suggestion that once they were on their feet they were free to go in whatever direction? What's the -- I'm just lost --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it done purposefully to maltreat the civilian population. It was just done because there was no other mean to transport them to another side of the -- of the line. They had to walk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What does that tell the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That it wasn't done purposefully to maltreat or harass civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm still lost, but put a question. We'll see what the follow-up questions will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of your investigation, did you come by information that between the confrontation lines there was a minefield?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Like all the confrontation lines during this war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view did there exist a possibility for the Serb buses to cross that stretch of the road which the civilians traversed on foot when they were on their way to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, it was a logic that the drop-off was before the confrontation line, and this is where, at least on 12 July, there was again separation of -- of men who ended up at the little school in Luka. And those allowed to cross, they crossed by foot, yes. Normal situation - I say normal - in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July there were members of the Dutch Battalion with the civilians in the column; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, as far as I know, indeed the UN personnel tried to escort the buses. At least a few of them then crossed the line. The others were seized of their vehicles and equipment, as far as I know. So they couldn't monitoring the process. There were blockades all along the road for various reasons, the witnesses will better explain, but there was no monitoring really of the situation by these UN forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, we did agree today, and we'll discuss the military column a bit. Did you come by information that would indicate how many armed persons were present in the column compared to those who made up the column overall?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it is a very rough estimate, what I usually say is that approximately one-third of this approximately 15.000-man column was armed. We can see on footage that among these armed men are also civilians carrying weapons. Approximately a third according to various testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, were you referring to 15.000 or 50.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fifteen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We established today that the column sustained losses. Did you establish what the losses were in the column that were sustained in combat? Do you have any information, and what does it indicate?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make it very easy, we -- I mean, I never attempted to count these battle casualties, because all of them are considered battle casualties whatever happened to them in the forest. As long as we do not frame them as being victims of a crime, we do not investigate the matter, and the military aspect of this operation is not the concern of the investigation. It's not the focus. We will consider all of them as legitimate battle casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So did you establish -- did you try to establish the number or not? If you didn't, say so.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say so. We didn't for the reasons I just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you establish at least where and which parts of the column sustained losses, major losses? I will have to repeat my question. Geographically speaking, along that route did you establish the locations where the column sustained losses?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In connection with the investigation, the main losses were the first ambush in the area above Kravica. This is connected with the investigation, because it's the following morning that the massive surrender process took place. As far as the military story of the column is concerned, as you know there was a separation of this column in order to move towards Zvornik and make a fake attempt to attack Zvornik, but this part has not at all been investigated because I put it in the frame of the military history of this thing, not in the frame of the criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were interviewing witnesses, did you come by information that the column sustained major losses already at Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is in fact the name of the location where the ambush took place, Kamenica being in the vicinity of Kravica but behind the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall now what the witnesses told you whom you interviewed, what the losses were? Is it correct that the figures range between a thousand and 2000?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it matches the findings of the Norwegian team I was talking about one hour ago, but again, all these persons killed in this area, including those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, if I -- if you do not mind, I would like to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was what the witnesses told you. Whether there's contradictory evidence is a different matter. That's perhaps your mindset as an investigator that you're thinking about these matters, but you're here as a witness of fact and you're asked what the witnesses told you in terms of number between a thousand and 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm or infirm what the witness says. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the witnesses also tell you about two ambushes at mount Udrc?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the episodes between 11.00/midnight and the 16 along the path of this column was not the topic of the investigation, but, yes, Udrc was a differ crossing point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned yourself the fighting around --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, the simple question was whether they told you about ambushes at mount Udrc, whether it was a difficult crossing point or not. Did they tell you about ambushes at that spot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ambushes, no. Difficult crossing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they perhaps tell you how -- or what were the losses that they sustained at that difficult crossing point?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also told us that you didn't know what the losses were in that important attack on Zvornik, although there was heavy fighting taking place there as well. You do know that.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may be a translation issue, but I don't think there's any history of an attack on Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [In English] Fake attack, as I think it was called.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A diversion. It was a diversion movement, but again this is the military history --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second. If first Mr. Lukic would repeat what he said after Mr. McCloskey intervened. Mr. McCloskey said, "I don't think there was any history of an attack in Zvornik," and then you said something, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I said "fake attack." And actually witness corrected me, it's "a diversion."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military terms is diversion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But again it's far away from this investigation we are discussing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, we have now a full record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note that they are having difficulty hearing Mr. Lukic, and the difference in the B/C/S words was in one letter only, hence the error, "vazan," as opposed to "lazan."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was also fighting on the very separation line or around it when the column was crossing onto the territory under the control of the BH Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade sustained rather heavy losses on that occasion, or, rather, heavier losses than it had ever sustained during the course of the entire war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I heard, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The colleague is telling me to emphasise that this is the Zvornik Brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska. You do know what sanitisation of terrain is; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It implies the collection of dead bodies following any sort of combat; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that process the army buries the dead. Would the army bury only its own dead or even the dead of the enemy, that's to say all of the dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I don't know. It's up to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the bodies would be buried in common graves in such occasions?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, again I'm trying to understand your line of questioning. Do you want to ask the witness simply whether he has investigated whether where mass graves were found, whether the investigation gave any support for the idea that they may have ended up there after the sanitation of the terrain? I can imagine that you would then have a focused discussion, for example, on the presence of shell casings around that mass grave. Well, there's a lot to be said about it, but is that what you're -- what you're -- what you want to establish? Then let's be clear on that. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you answer the questions raised by Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the only option you have is this one, to say that these people we found are battle casualty, that we leave it to the experts to explain. This is not the case, and what I could add is just that if you look indeed at the terrain, at the distances, at the dates, to me what -- this theory is useless. It's not true. All this investigation, all the forensics show very clearly what the path of these prisoners was. I think it's very well reconstructed, but I understand that there is a need to say that tease people with blindfolds and ligatures are battle casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is not our case. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep matters short. Do I understand your answer to be, Mr. Ruez, that on the basis of the investigations not only by you but also by colleagues and experts, that a lot of facts were established which would contradict an explanation of the situation as the persons found in mass graves to be collected during a process of sanitation only? Is that, in brief, what you want to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is absolutely right, but I'm talking only about the graves we show during these trials. If other graves come up from other sources, Bosniak sources, for example, they are not under investigation. I would personally not meld them with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- this process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say if we understand this answer in this way, it would apply only to the graves you have investigated. Mr. Lukic, does this clarify the matter for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'll just have one or two follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm also looking at the clock. If -- I think we started a bit late, but in order to have some time left after, if you would do the one or two follow-up questions now and then we take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned ligatures and blindfolds. What did your investigation reveal? How many people of the 6.000 that you just mentioned had their hands tied and blindfolds on?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will leave this to the expert witnesses who will come here to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do not know as a witness whether they will come or not. That's for the parties to decide. But you'd say you'd rather leave answers to those questions to those who investigated in detail those matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Who already testified in all the previous trials. That's why I allow myself to say that. They will or maybe they already came, I don't follow this trial aside my own testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have -- I mean, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, do you know the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then a simple no would have done right from the beginning. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know -- did you establish in the course of your investigation that there were bodies of different degrees of decomposition found in the same grave?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a detail I do not know, and I leave it to the experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That were my follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we take a break first. Could the witness already follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I've been thinking a lot about the previous issue where I said I was lost. I think I now do understand it and I think the following simple question would have done: Witness, those who had to walk for the last part of reaching the other territory, did you form an opinion about that was harassment or whether it was inevitable due to the fact that they had to cross no man's land with all the risks of that and where they could not be accompanied by the soldiers? Then I would have understood what the issue was you were raising. We finally have to make up our mind on the basis of the evidence, so the clearer you present it, the better we'll be able to evaluate it. We take a break, and we resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I'd like to raise the following issue: On the 23rd of April, the Defence has filed a request for an extension of time to file its Rule 94 bis (B) notice in response to the Prosecution's 28th of March, 2013, notice of disclosure of the expert report of Dr. Helge Brunborg. In the request it submits that the Defence expert is still in the process of analysing the material provided by the Prosecution, adding that, moreover, it has not yet received B/C/S translations of two figures accompanying the expert reports. Any problem in the request being granted, and when do you think the B/C/S would be provided to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Lukic, when I asked him, gave me the exact numbers of those tables a few days ago and we have sent them to be translated and we should have them any day. So that shouldn't be problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest at this moment the Chamber will grant the requested relief, and we set the deadline provisionally in the expectation, Mr. Lukic, that the B/C/S material will arrive soon. We set the deadline for a Rule 94 bis (B) response to the 14th of May, and if anything unexpected happens, of course you can address the Chamber again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You now may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you mentioned the Norwegians to us. Do you know how many bodies they collected in total and in which area?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They operated in the area of Kamenica. I don't know how many bodies were collected. What I do know is that they have left many since two years later I did request to SFOR at that time to have an overflight by helicopter, and they brought back a film where obviously human remains were still very obviously in the area. So they didn't collect all the bodies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You cannot give us an approximation as to the number of bodies that had been collected by the Norwegians?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters did not hear the end of Mr. Lukic's sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us the total number of bodies collected by the Norwegians and the number of bodies that you saw or discovered later when flying in that area, as you said.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the number. We stayed disconnected from this team since they were operating on humanitarian ground, and this area being a battle area was out of the frame of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 16th of April the Muslim forces launched a counter-attack against the Serb forces? Is that correct? Is that something that is separate from the breakthrough itself of the line, that is, to help the breakthrough of the 28th Division, or is this a separate battle, if you will?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 16th of April. Which year, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1995, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are we talking about April or July?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I made a mistake. 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Nezuk indeed was the breakthrough, the 16, which was not really a breakthrough since the Serb side opened the line for the column to exit according to some deal with the Serb prisoners without entering the details again. This is, for me, part of the military history of the situation but not part of the criminal investigation since I have all reasons to believe that the bodies of these battles are to be found but not in the graves under investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you rule out that possibility or are you making an assumption?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I rule it out for three reasons: The geographic location of the graves we exposed; the dates in connection with the records of the engineer battalion of the Zvornik Brigade; and because of all these forensic elements. So for these three reasons, I totally disconnect the sites that we are presenting here in court with possible sanitary and burials that occurred at one stage or another in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A geographic reason can be overcome by transport; isn't that right? Sorry. And a time objection would not be proper if we're looking at secondary graves; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secondary grave aspect will have to be separate from always, but if you take Lazete, for example, the witnesses say that the execution during the night took place when the heavy equipment was already burying part of the grave. So thinking that these bodies would be at the same moment when the battle at Nezuk -- buried and in Lazete, sorry, but I cannot tell you what I think of that. I mean it's -- for me it is such a nonsense that I don't want to be too radical in my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the focus of the testimony of this witness was and should be, I tried to remind the Prosecution various times and I remind you now as well, is not what conclusions he drew from these matters and what happened but, rather, what he found during his investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think all my questions have that caveat, that I always ask the witness even at the beginning when he asked me would I want his assumption, I said, No, I want the result of your investigation. But I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ruez, did you find out during your investigations that about 1.000 soldiers from Srebrenica broke through to Zepa and then crossed over to Serbia from there, or did you not deal with this at all?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These 1.000 are not to be found in the graves that we connect with the capture and assassination of the prisoners. The only thing that involved interest for us and for me and for the Prosecution linked with this movement of people towards Zepa is that one of the survivors of the Kravica warehouse fled to Zepa. And this is the reason why he survived, because being captured in Zepa he was not identified as coming from Srebrenica and ended up at the last prisoner exchange in March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In brief, your answer would be, "We were not dealing with it," right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Totally out of the frame of the criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you addressing the fighting that broke out between one stretch of the column and another stretch of the column where people were not aware of the fact that they were part of the same column?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but they will be counted among the battle casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since they --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, how is that distinction made? Apart from 400-odd bodies that had ligatures on them, how would you distinguish between someone who was killed in combat and someone who was executed?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, from this path that leads from the moment the person has been captured or has surrendered then taken to a detention location, then taken to an execution area, and the burial process and the forensic linked with it, plus the dates that we know the heavy equipment was sent to bury these bodies, all this, in my view, excludes the possibility that the graves we are talking about are graves filled with battle casualties collected on the ground for sanitarian reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We said that in the course of your investigation you relied upon the assistance of experts from different fields. Is it correct that experts in forensics were not able to make that distinction with this certainty and to ascertain who the persons were who were killed in combat as opposed to those who were executed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think there is a basic misunderstanding here. What the witness says is: Our investigation was focused on people, let's keep it simple, found in the mass graves or at the least the larger graves, people that had surrendered or were captured, then taken to this place, et cetera. What you are saying now is that the forensic experts not always were able to make the distinction between those who died in combat and those who, for example, were -- indications were found by ligature or whatever. So you are referring to the group which is part of the investigation. The witness told us, and that was how it started, that whoever may have died in the column, not having surrendered, not having -- whatever happened there, right or wrong, would be considered combat casualties for very practical purposes. Whether they were or not is a different matter, but at least that's how they were considered. The witness also has told us that he, on the basis of the investigation, he considered it to be excluded for good or bad reasons. You can further explore that, that those found in the mass graves were taken there as a result of sanitation measures. And, of course, if you are killed somewhere before having surrendered, before having -- having being captured, then you would be found somewhere and then on the basis of sanitation -- explain to us why he considers it unlikely or that people that ended up in the graves he investigated. Now, that story gives an answer to the question at least, but let's see what Mr. Ruez says, that even, and I take it you are referring to forensic pathologist or forensic -- you said only "forensic." There are a lot of forensic sciences other than -- but they have apparently examined the bodies found somewhere and were not able on the basis of their expertise to establish whether they were casualties of combat or not, so therefore you cannot rely on them to draw any conclusions, and I understood from Mr. Ruez that then often conclusions were drawn, right or wrong, on other sources, testimonies, whatever. But what the forensic pathologists found in those graves is something which is not part -- that in Mr. Ruez's explanation cannot be people coming from what happened in the column. So, therefore, I do not see how you can mix up the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm mixing up anything but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then put a clear question which shows that you're not mixing up anything. Because the casualties in the column are not the bodies Mr. Ruez explained us to be found in the graves he -- that were the subject of his investigations. These are two different categories. And, Mr. Ruez, unless I misunderstood your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It's a perfect summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not here to summarise testimony, but, Mr. Lukic, put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I can explain myself a bit further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you put the right questions I'll not intervene. I mean, with the right questions, of course you choose yourself, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is my question: How is it possible that in the secondary graves, we're not talking about primary graves now, only about the secondary graves, how is it possible that one can be sure that such a grave does not contain the bodies of those who were killed in battle?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I insist again on the fact that there will be an expert coming who will develop at length all the forensic details that enable us to confirm that the bodies found in the secondary graves are coming from the primary graves that have been disturbed end of September, beginning of October 1995. So by adding the leftover of the primary graves with what is found in the secondary graves, connecting them we end up with a final number of persons executed on each of these execution sites we went through during my direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me keep this short as well. I do understand that your answer is that experts -- that you learned that experts are able to explain why such a conclusion can be drawn. That's simply --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can put it like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we'll wait for the expert to appear. Let me ask you a question about identity documents. Is it correct that you and members of your investigation team came to the conclusion that most of the soldiers, members of the 28th Division in Srebrenica, discarded all the items that could possibly identify them as combatants?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was not under investigation. Most certainly some did it for whatever reason, but this was not under investigation. Again, at the end if the prisoners are military or civilians, they are prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'll have to just try again to remind you. I'll call 1D858 in the e-court. 1D858, and we need page 48. We need lines 19 through 25, actually, through 23, and I'll quote: "Q. Sir, with respect to these identification cards, isn't it true that you in your investigation or you as the investigator in charge of this team have concluded 'most of the soldiers were getting rid of any element which could identify them as combatants,' correct? "A. Yes, correct."

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, okay. You know, not only the military, but I believe others also. I will not enter in weird details regarding this aspect, but in some instances several IDs were found in -- hidden in a place where no one would find them on one person. Not being identified was indeed a concern for most of these men who were fleeing, because they -- they were fleeing. They had reasons to flee, sometimes because they were combatants, sometimes because they were just horribly scared due to their previous experience in the area since 1992, and so on and so on. But at the end of the day, it's the DNA that is of interest for us in order to identify who is who based on the missing book of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DNA analysis, I don't know if you heard it from your colleagues, does not point to the manner of death. It only establishes identity.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And the cause of death, as you know, is always multiple gunshot wounds. This makes it indeed difficult to compare someone killed in combat with someone killed by a firing squad, but again it's the full chronology of these individuals that begs the difference between someone who has been assassinated and someone who died in combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, when you were asked by Mr. Lukic whether the investigation team came to the conclusion that most of the soldiers, members of the 28th Division in Srebrenica, discarded all the items that could possibly identify them as combatants, you said "No," and at least you explained why the answer was no. And then a part of the testimony was put to you with exactly the same language where during that testimony you answered, "Yes, correct," and then you started explaining other things. It seems to be contradictory. It may be that you would have wanted to say more or to further explain, but at least what you say today is 180 degrees opposite to what you said when you said in that other case, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I disagree. If you read back my first instinctive answer, I said, "No, maybe many did," and so on, because I was not focused on the topic for the simple reason that to me this is not of high importance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt, Mr. Ruez. Which is the instinctive answer which we must look at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first answer when I said "No," and then thinking it through I added something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In today's testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Today, yes. Well, one would, I think, very easily understand in the circumstances of this period of time that an individual fleeing the Bosnian Serb Army was not necessarily willing to flag off his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- let me see again. One second, please. You were asked about the conclusions of the investigation team in both questions, at the time and now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you said, "Yes, that is correct," and today you say -- and that's not saying what happened or what didn't happen. You were asked about whether the conclusions of the team at the time were that most of the soldiers were getting rid of any elements which could identify them as combatants. At the time you said, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it's right or wrong, but that was the conclusion. Today you said, "No." You added to that that many may have done so, but you denied that this was the conclusion of the investigation. You even explained that it was not part of the investigation, and that contradicts what you said in the previous case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perfect. Let's take it as a contradiction. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Well, Mr. Lukic, when I say please proceed, it is -- we are already beyond quarter past 2.00. Mr. McCloskey, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I -- just we find ourselves with a logistic situation. I have not spoken to Mr. Ruez and his ability to come back, and I don't know, perhaps Your Honours have a preference when he does come back. Does Mr. Lukic need him to come back, which I assume based on his time-frame he may.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have less than one hour, in between half an hour or an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour. I don't have, off the top of my head, the schedule for next week. Would there be any problem in starting on Wednesday with the last half hour of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The -- well, aside -- I don't know Mr. Ruez's -- his police schedule. We do have our last two DutchBat soldiers, I believe a private and a general, both who have Dutch interpreters reserved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. Lukic, you -- most likely then it would be at a later date after.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whenever it suits the witness and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, I know France is at a distance, but would you be willing to come back and do you have any -- could you please communicate with the Victims and Witness Section, not with the Prosecution but Victims and Witness Section, whether you have any dates where you would not be available or whether you have any dates of preference so that we could hear the last part of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will stay available to the Defence as soon as we can fix a date with the witness unit, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would please then do that. And most likely it will not be next week then because the first two days we're not sitting, and after that we have interpreters. Then I have again to instruct you, Mr. Ruez, that you should not talk about your testimony or communicate in any other way with whomever, and then you may now follow the usher and we would like to see you back soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any other matters to be raised before we adjourn? If not, we adjourn for the day with apologies for the late finish to everyone who is suffering under it, and we will resume Wednesday, the 1st of May, in this same Courtroom I at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of May, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.
